Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Education | National NAGRAT calls for rigorous system to regulate early BECE, describes two-year ban as harsh Source : Prince Adu-Owusu 26 November 2026 7:59pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) has called for a rigorous system to regulate the early progression of pupils to higher classes, describing the Education Ministry’s two-year ban on early BECE candidates as too harsh.
NAGRAT President, Jacob Anaba, said that although pupils should ordinarily go through all the stages of the educational curriculum, exceptions may be necessary for learners who demonstrate exceptional academic ability.
Speaking on JoyFM’s Top Story on Thursday, November 26, he explained that learning is tied to particular age groups, which informs how the national curriculum is structured.
He said allowing pupils to skip classes without properly assessing their readiness could deprive them of essential academic knowledge, foundational skills, and important social and psychological experiences.
“Research has indicated and/or shown that learning comes with a particular age. That is why when curriculum is developed, it’s developed to meet the age brackets. So, it is very important that when learners go to school, they go through the whole process or the stages,” he said.
Mr Anaba, however, acknowledged that some pupils may need to advance to higher classes earlier than scheduled, but insisted that such decisions must be guided by a rigorous assessment system.
“However, if a student needs to be skipped or to move to another grade, there must be a very good rigorous system to ensure that we are able to determine that that student can learn in the next stage,” he said.
He criticised the blanket nature of the Education Ministry’s directive, arguing that a two-year restriction could have unintended consequences for pupils who are otherwise academically prepared to advance.
“So the ban was so harsh. In fact, what the Ministry should have done was to institute a system to ensure that we move gradually to make sure that there are systems in place to check these things,” he said.
Mr Anaba also raised concerns about the impact of removing academically strong pupils from their schools, saying their presence often encourages other learners to improve their performance.
He explained that transferring such pupils to other schools to sit the BECE could affect the overall performance of their former classmates.
He further warned that teachers could lose motivation if the more academically challenging pupils were removed from their classrooms.
“Teachers want challenging students in their classroom. So, if such challenging students are taken away from their class, then the teachers also lose motivation,” he said.
Mr Anaba called for the establishment of appropriate mechanisms to assess pupils before allowing them to skip classes, stressing that the process must ensure that learners are adequately prepared for the next stage of their education.
